claims.text: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy contains dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries.
Internal lamellar boundaries are prone to microcrack initiation during tensile deformation.
Adding approximately 0.1–0.5 at.% boron during melting will cause boron to segregate to lamellar interfaces during solidification and homogenization.
Boron segregation will enhance cohesion at dual-phase lamellar colony boundaries.
Enhanced interfacial cohesion will minimize localized embrittlement.
Enhanced interfacial cohesion will delay microcrack initiation.
Boron atoms have a propensity to segregate to high-energy interfaces.
Boron at lamellar boundaries reduces local stress concentrations during tensile loading.
Boron at lamellar boundaries mitigates microcrack initiation during tensile loading.
Retarded crack propagation enables increased strain hardening while maintaining or enhancing strength.
The boron-modified alloy will have higher room-temperature tensile strength than the unmodified lamellar baseline.
The boron-modified alloy will have greater room-temperature elongation than the unmodified lamellar baseline.
The unmodified alloy has high strength but limited room-temperature ductility.
The baseline alloy's limited ductility is primarily caused by microcrack initiation at internal boundaries between dual-phase lamellae.
The intervention is effective only if boron preferentially segregates rather than forming deleterious boride phases.
Beneficial effects require boron content and processing conditions that do not detrimentally alter the lamellar structure.
Excessive boron or inappropriate heat treatment could produce unwanted phases.
